name: Saulteaux Ojibwe
confidence_why: Miller 2018, from recordings of eight Manitoba Saulteaux speakers, found only a consistent word-final prominence and no reliable primary or secondary stress, against the older three-rule account of Voorhis 1976 and Cote 1985 (repeated by Logan 2001 and Cote 2012) under which every long vowel, every final syllable and every second short-vowel syllable is stressed, and since Miller herself leaves open whether Saulteaux is a final-stress language or has no word stress at all, the type of system is under active debate with no acoustic study to settle it.

catalog_quote: [Miller 2018:127-130] Final Prominence (whatever its source) is confirmed in Saulteaux nouns (213) and verbs (214) both in isolation and within a sentence (215). Impressionistically, this prominence is marked by a rise in pitch and intensity. ... Beyond this final prominence, stress assignment in Saulteaux Ojibwe has proven elusive. ... The two approaches make different predictions for stress assignment, but testing shows neither approach's predictions are borne out in Saulteaux. ... In fact, there is no consistent acoustic evidence for either primary or secondary stress in Saulteaux regardless of the predictions above. Some syllables may sound more prominent, but their location is not predictable from item to item. ... Perhaps Saulteaux Ojibwe is, in fact, a final stress language. It is just as likely to be a boundary phenomenon, however. As there is no clear way to decide between the two analyses, it remains open to future research. || [Logan 2001:11] The placement of stress in Ojibwa (including Saulteaux) can be satisfactorily explained in a fairly straightforward fashion and there can be several stressed syllables within a word. There are three basic rules for stress assignment (as put forward by Voorhis et al 1976 and Cote 1984): 1) Each syllable with a long vowel will be stressed. 2) The last syllable of every word is obligatorily stressed. 3) Every second syllable in a sequence of syllables with short vowels will be stressed.

new_statements.rule_in_words: The one consistent prominence is on the final syllable of every word (noun or verb, in isolation and in running speech), realized as a rise in pitch and intensity; Miller cannot decide whether this is final word stress or a boundary effect. The traditional description (Logan 2001:11 after Voorhis 1976 and Cote 1984, also in Cote 2012:15) is a quantity-sensitive alternating system: every long-vowel syllable is stressed, the last syllable is always stressed, and every second syllable in the compilation of short-vowel syllables is stressed, with the remaining short vowels reduced or elided; no primary stress is singled out. Miller, listening to 24 h of recordings from eight speakers, found no consistent primary or secondary stress matching either the traditional or Hayes' iambic predictions, and retains iambic feet only to account for optional weak-vowel syncope. If a single positional reading is required, fixed: final syllable is the only pattern both sources agree on; weight-sensitive (iambic) is the traditional rule.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Miller 2018: no consistent acoustic evidence for primary or secondary stress; left-to-right iambic foot structure still motivated by optional syncope of foot-weak short vowels (mostly pronominal clitics). Logan 2001:11: several stressed syllables per word (all long-vowel syllables plus every second short-vowel syllable), no primary/secondary distinction made.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. Logan notes unstressed short vowels are elided far less than in eastern dialects (Odawa). Miller notes results are impressionistic and that an acoustic study is still needed.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level: nouns and verbs in citation form and inside sentences (Miller exx. 213-215). Miller's Table 5.1 places Final Prominence at the right edge of the whole verb complex (including the object-number clitic) and at the end of each root of a compound; Logan's rule is stated for 'every word'.
new_statements.identity_note: ojw / west1510 = Saulteaux (Plains or Western Ojibwe) of Manitoba and Saskatchewan. Miller 2018's data are from eight Manitoba speakers born in Berens River, Roseau River, Gypsumville, Hollow Water, Sandy Bay and Duck Bay (Lake Winnipeg / Interlake area); Valentine's dialectology puts Berens River in a northern (Berens River/Northwestern, cf. ojb nort2961) group, but Miller labels the whole sample Saulteaux. Logan 2001 (the traditional rule) is based on speakers from the Cote and Muscowpetung reserves in Saskatchewan, squarely ojw. Tallman 2011 = Manitoba Saulteaux; Cote 2012 = Cote First Nation, Saskatchewan.
